toc.title: Be a partner in your own treatment

sections.title: Sharing a language, not imposing one

toc.title: It's just you, and that's enough

blocks.p: Over the last three episodes I've talked about how you don't have parts, you're not reparenting yourself, you don't have a shadow, and you don't have an ego. These are all psychological concepts that can act as metaphors and be helpful, but they're not real things. Here I want to talk about what you're left with when you take them away: yourself. And how that's enough, but also pretty darn terrifying.
My hope is that you get some clarity about yourself, a little bit of challenge, and maybe some more self-belief that you can handle things you didn't think you could.
These concepts have a place as metaphors, as top-down state regulators as far as the Polyvagal Theory is concerned. That is their role, and in my opinion it shouldn't go beyond that.

If you believe you actually do have parts, unless you're diagnosed with or living with DID, or that there's actually a shadow somewhere inside of you, I don't know what that means. But if that's you, then you're operating in the realm of belief, and that's completely fine. It's just different from taking on a metaphor as a tool to help you in your own self-regulation. Belief versus metaphor is a pretty important distinction.
I don't want to disregard these things altogether. They can be helpful. But I really want to encourage you to ask: what are these things, and how do they apply to me?
Ultimately, I want you to have clarity in what you're being taught by others, and that includes me. If people aren't explaining clearly what they mean, I think they're doing you a disservice.

Take puzzle self therapy. It's not real. I made it up. When I laid it out more on Instagram, it seemed like some people didn't quite get that, and a couple of comments concerned me. So if I ever bring it up again, I'll say up front, "This is not real." It serves a purpose: it shows how easy it is to come up with metaphors for our consciousness, or whatever that might be, and how they can be simply made up, with no grounding in evidence.

So I think those of us who are Instagram people and podcast therapists and whatnot have to be honest and clear in what we're saying. If you want to espouse ideas around ego and shadow and reparenting and parts, fine. But do you mean that literally, or as a metaphor?

If you mean it as a metaphor, people can join you on it. It's not you at the top of a mountain sharing your wisdom. It's you saying, "Hey, I have an idea," and someone else saying, "Yes, that works for me," or, "No, it doesn't." When we pronounce as experts, "Here's reality, you have a puzzle inside of you," the people who rely on us, or trust us because we've already helped them, might take that as literal truth. In my opinion, that gives them less power over these ideas, less equality. There's less joining, less understanding that these are metaphors we can use together.

I've never heard anyone else talk like this, and it's kind of disappointing, because it seems pretty damn obvious. When I tell my clients they have parts, what am I actually saying? When I think in terms of shadows, what does that mean? Is there evidence for it? Is it a truth claim or a metaphor? So I want to put this way of thinking out in the world, for you to use if you want. If it doesn't work for you, that's fine. You can rule it out of your toolbox of top-down cognitive state regulation techniques.

blocks.h: Be a partner in your own treatment

blocks.p: Another reason: I want you to be able to question the psychological concepts people put out there. I want you to be a partner in your own mental health treatment.

I want you to find a therapist who thinks in ways that excite you, or that complement the way you think. Challenge is completely fine too. The way I'm speaking right now might be challenging for you, and that doesn't mean it can't be helpful. If you were looking for a therapist and saw someone saying things like this, it might rub you wrong, but if you're curious, that could be an avenue to pursue with someone licensed in your area. Maybe you need someone more empathetic. Maybe you need someone more pushy and rah-rah. Maybe it's something you're not getting elsewhere in your life that you can get from a therapist in a professional way.

Or maybe you already know what you want. People have reached out to me saying, "I want some sort of somatic treatment. I don't want to do just talk therapy," and they seek me out. They know what they want, and they go find it. You might want parts work or shadow work or whatever the popular thing is, and you go find it, and that's cool. I just want you to feel empowered when you do. Ideally, I don't want you to show up to a therapist and accept whatever they tell you as gospel truth. I know there are limitations around insurance and whatnot, but you get the idea.

If you and your therapist agree that these aren't just metaphors, that you truly have parts, and the two of you are working on that shared agreement, good luck to you. At least you're more in the driver's seat of your own treatment.

blocks.h3: Sharing a language, not imposing one

blocks.p: Therapy is a cooperative process. In my opinion, it shouldn't be a therapist telling you, "This is the nature of your consciousness, and you have to think this way to benefit from treatment with me."

I want my clients to share a language with me, share concepts, and share goals. But those concepts need to be appropriate and fit what the client wants. I never tell my clients how to think. I may throw a red flag and say, "Hold up, let's pause on that." If they think they have parts, I might ask, "What do you mean by that?" so I understand the language they're using. But I would never tell them, "You can't talk like that in sessions with me," or "You have to think of yourself as a singular consciousness." Nor would I tell them they have to think of themselves as subpersonalities or shadows.
It's completely possible I'll work with someone whose way of thinking just won't fit with mine. If someone is looking for parts work, I'm not the therapist for them, and that's okay.

I don't even talk about the Polyvagal Theory with all my clients. Most of them honestly aren't interested. Some seek me out because of it, but for the most part people just want a therapist they feel comfortable with. I'll recommend things that might help us share language, but if they don't want that, I meet them where they're at.

I had one client who brought up how "a part of her" felt a certain way. I said, "Hold on. Just so I understand where you're coming from, what do you mean by that?" She said, "Well, aren't there, like, parts, internal family stuff?" She had just sort of heard these concepts. I said, "I can meet you on that if that's what you like, but let me tell you what I'm hearing when you say that." I did my much simpler method from the last episode, and she said, "Yeah, that makes a lot more sense to me. We don't need the parts stuff." So we didn't use it.

I want clients to have a lot of choice when they're seeking out a therapist, and to know there are other ways of thinking. Not all of us rely on these vague, abstract, non-evidenced psychological concepts. I'm raising my hand: there's at least one of us out here who rejects these ideas. And I think that what you bring to therapy, you already have what you need, and we can build on that.

So here's what I invite you to do. If you're fuming at me and this isn't clicking, you're invited to hang out and listen, but this honestly might not be a good fit for you. And this isn't for everybody. Some people wrote to me and said, "I need these concepts," and that's fine. Then this exercise isn't for you, so don't do it unless you can handle it.

For everyone else: what if I could take these ideas away from you? Take all of it out of your memory or your knowledge or your consciousness, wherever you want to put it: the parts, the reparenting, the ego, the shadow, fill in the blank. What if we started from scratch, with no idea what consciousness is, and just worked with what you have, and worked our way up from there?
First, let's leave it there. What does that feel like?
And then: what are you left with?

I ask my clients something similar pretty often, about the things that act as top-down cognitive state regulation, automatic thinking, or behaviors. If I could take away the addiction, the cutting, the thoughts of self-loathing, the ruminating on what someone did or didn't do, what would you be left with? It usually brings up something like, "Oh God, that's where all my painful stuff is." So I'm asking you the same thing, but about these psychological concepts.

To me, you're left with yourself. Not parts, not subpersonalities you have to wonder about and evaluate and figure out and rationalize and track with your mind. It's you. And that might be terrifying.
When I first started thinking this way, there was this sense of, "Oh God, it's me." A sense of smallness. A kind of cognition of, "Oh, fuck."

Especially because I'm an atheist. I don't believe I have a soul. I don't think I go anywhere after I die. I think this is it. We're not getting into that here, but for me there's a whole other layer of, "It is just me, and this is just it."

I think these concepts can act as buffers, or bumpers. Instead of feeling and thinking about that "oh, fuck," we use the bumpers to dampen the impact. When I take away all of these concepts, there's this intense awareness of what's happening within me, and I wonder if you'll have the same experience. If those concepts aren't true, where else do you go besides what's happening within you? For me, there's me, and there's the world, and that's about it.
So this idea may be daunting. It might be big and scary. It was for me at first. I don't quite feel like that anymore. Or maybe I do, but now it's more a feeling of appreciation and responsibility.

If I took away those psychological concepts from you as a provider, what would you be left with? If you didn't get to rely on these fun, wonderful, but made-up explanations of consciousness, would you be able to sit with that?

These ideas might help you connect with your clients more, and that's great. But I wonder if they act as a bumper that makes it easier to sit with your client's distress, or with your own distress in session, the anxiety of being a therapist. I'm just going to put that out there, and it may really upset you.

blocks.h: It's just you, and that's enough

blocks.p: By the end of this series, I'll probably have upset the majority of my audience. Plus mentioning being an atheist. This might be where we part ways, and that does sadden me.

Here's the core idea some people did not like: "It's just you." I'm sorry, but it is, and I'm going to double down on it. I'm not talking about atheism and God here. That's a whole separate discussion. As far as these psychological concepts go, it's just you. You can use them as metaphors to help you regulate your state. Cool. But other than that, it's just you.

And that's enough. You are enough, in my opinion. You have enough within you to get unstuck. I really believe that. You may not know it. You may not believe it. You may not yet be able to access all the tools you have within you, or all those sensations, or all that stuckness. And of course it's good to learn more. But I do believe that within you, you have what you need to get more unstuck.
So the aim is to get to know yourself more for what you have and what you're bringing to the table in this very moment. A metaphorical table. There's no consciousness table.

What do you have right now, after I've taken away all those psychological concepts? That is enough. There's a lot there to work with, for therapists and for yourself in your own self-work. I don't need you to believe you have parts. That's not the way I work as a therapist.

We don't know what consciousness is. We don't. But we don't need multiple pieces of consciousness to explain consciousness. That doesn't make sense. I love this field, and the practice of therapy. In my opinion, there has to be a balance to all these psychological concepts people think up to explain consciousness: something out there that says, "No." That's what I'm trying to do here.

So I encourage you to sit with that, and with the discomfort that might already be in you, if you can. If you can't, that's okay, and maybe the psychological concepts can help you get there eventually.

If a metaphor helps you stay with it, use it. You can do the whole puzzle thing: imagine there's a puzzle piece missing inside of you, and imagine what the missing space feels like. That's totally fine. But eventually, sitting with your discomfort is the goal. Here's how I see it unfolding, as you're ready:

ol: Sit with your discomfort. If you need a top-down metaphor to do that, fine.
If you can do that, you can also sit with these feelings just as they are, just as you are right now.
Then that feeling, that sensation, will tell you what to do next. There will be a little impulse inside of you about what should happen next.
And at some point there may be some appreciation for simply being alive, for sitting with yourself and taking in the you-ness of being you.

blocks.p: It is just you. That's completely okay, and that is enough.

I want transparency and clarity about what I'm doing here, too. My role is to act as a resource to help you eventually be able to be with what's inside of you with curiosity and without judgment, without evaluation, without applying different cognitive layers. Just simply feeling what's inside of you.

I don't want to be a dispenser of psychological concepts that I make up, and I don't want to use other people's made-up concepts either. I'd love to be a resource for whatever goal you have for yourself. I'm continually trying to refine my understanding of the Polyvagal Theory, I'd love to learn more about attachment, and I've been spending more and more time trying to understand what the heck consciousness is, if anything. I want to learn things and bring them back to you, like a translator.

But I also want you to challenge what you're learning, and that includes me. Look at what you're taking in and ask yourself: "Is this a description of reality, or is this a metaphor that I can actively use?" Either can be okay. I just want you to be an active participant in your therapy, and as a consumer of mental health information. There's so much out there that you really have to be active in it, and ask really tough questions.
